opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, MERL was a really interesting place when I joined. I came out of my PhD at the University of Maryland, and MERL was one of those classic industrial research labs, in the tradition of places like Bell Labs or Xerox PARC, but smaller and more focused. It was in Cambridge, Massachusetts, right next to MIT and Harvard, so there was a strong academic feel to it.

What I appreciated was that researchers had a lot of freedom. You were expected to publish at top venues like CVPR and ICCV, and the bar was quite high. At the same time, because it's the research arm of Mitsubishi Electric, there was always the question of how your work might eventually connect to the company's products: factory automation, robotics, elevators, automotive systems, things like that. So you learned to think about real-world problems, not just benchmarks.

In computer vision especially, MERL had a very strong reputation. There were senior researchers there who had done foundational work, and being around them taught me a lot about how to pick problems and how to do rigorous research. The lab was small enough that you could talk to almost anyone, and people were very generous with their time.

Of course, there were limitations too. Compared to the big tech companies, the compute resources and team sizes were modest, and this was right around when deep learning was taking off. Things started moving very fast and scale became more and more important. So for me, MERL was a wonderful place to grow as an independent researcher, but over time I felt the field shifting toward places that could invest heavily in large-scale learning, and that eventually influenced my decision to move on.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, when I joined MERL right after my PhD, I thought of it as a very special kind of place. It's small — maybe eighty or so researchers at the time — but it had this long tradition. It was founded in the early nineties in Cambridge, right next to MIT, and historically it had been one of the strongest industrial labs in computer vision and graphics. A lot of classic work came out of there. The Viola–Jones face detector, for example, was done at MERL. So the reputation in the vision community was very good.

What I appreciated most was the freedom. It was a Japanese company's lab, but the Cambridge office ran in a very academic way. You were expected to publish, go to conferences, build your own agenda. Nobody told me, "this quarter you need to ship this feature." The expectation was more like: do good research, and once in a while, find a way to connect it to something Mitsubishi Electric cares about — factory automation, robotics, automotive, elevators. And those connections were real. I worked on things like bin picking for industrial robots, 3D pose estimation, and that grounded my research in actual physical problems, which I think shaped how I think even today.

At the same time, I'd be honest about the limitations. It was a smaller lab, resources were modest compared to what a big American tech company could offer, and this was right around the time deep learning started taking off — 2012, 2013. You could feel that the center of gravity was shifting toward places with huge compute and data. For a lab like MERL, that was hard to keep up with. So for me it was a wonderful place to grow as an independent researcher, to learn how to pick problems and finish them, but after a few years I felt that if I wanted to work on the frontier of deep learning at scale, I needed to be somewhere with more resources. That's eventually what led me to NVIDIA.
